name: Lamotrigine
summary: A broad-spectrum sodium-channel-blocking anticonvulsant with a favorable cognitive profile, used for focal and generalized seizures and bipolar maintenance.
mechanism: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in a use-dependent manner and reduces glutamate release, stabilizing neuronal membranes.

pharmacokinetics.halfLife: 25–33 h (monotherapy); ~15 h with enzyme inducers; ~60–70 h with valproate
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic glucuronidation (UGT), no significant CYP involvement

dosing.adult: Start 25 mg/day × 2 weeks, then 50 mg/day × 2 weeks, then increase gradually (monotherapy); with valproate, start 25 mg every other day and titrate half-speed
dosing.maxDose: 400 mg/day monotherapy (higher doses used with enzyme-inducing co-medications)
dosing.renalAdjustment: Reduce dose in severe renal impairment

safety.pregnancy: Some studies suggest a small increase in oral cleft risk; not clearly teratogenic — do not abruptly stop in epilepsy without specialist advice
contraindications: Prior severe hypersensitivity reaction (e.g., SJS/TEN) to lamotrigine
warnings: Serious rash/SJS/TEN — risk is highest with rapid titration or concurrent valproate
Any unexplained new rash in the first 8 weeks warrants stopping and evaluation
Class warning: suicidal thoughts and behavior
safety.overdose: Ataxia, nystagmus, seizures, coma; high doses can widen QRS; supportive care

clinicalPearls: Never titrate fast — the SJS/TEN risk is titration-related; with valproate, halve the starting dose and double the titration interval
Valproate roughly doubles lamotrigine's half-life — expect significantly higher levels when the two are combined
good: Focal and generalized seizures with a clean cognitive profile; bipolar maintenance.
bad: Anyone who cannot reliably follow the slow titration schedule, or patients on valproate without careful dose adjustment.

provenance.notes: Curated from standard neurology/pharmacology references. Values omitted where not confidently known — nothing invented.
